headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiology of Diabetes in Pregnancy
headings.content: Diabetes mellitus during pregnancy represents a significant metabolic challenge that requires careful understanding by nursing students in Nigeria. During normal pregnancy, maternal physiology undergoes adaptations to ensure an adequate supply of glucose to the developing fetus. In early pregnancy, insulin sensitivity increases, but as gestation progresses, placental hormones such as human placental lactogen (hPL), cortisol, progesterone, and prolactin induce progressive peripheral insulin resistance. This diabetogenic state ensures high postprandial glucose levels available for fetal transport across the placenta. In healthy women, pancreatic beta-cells compensate by increasing insulin secretion. However, in women with compromised beta-cell function or pre-existing insulin resistance, this compensatory mechanism fails, leading to maternal hyperglycemia. Chronic maternal hyperglycemia results in excessive glucose transfer to the fetus. The fetal pancreas responds by hypersecreting insulin, an anabolic hormone that drives excessive fetal growth, fat deposition, and organomegaly. Understanding this pathophysiology is crucial for nurses managing antenatal clients, as it explains why maternal blood glucose directly impacts fetal well-being, birth weight, and immediate neonatal outcomes. Recognizing these hormonal shifts helps clinicians anticipate when glucose intolerance is most likely to manifest or worsen during the gestational timeline.

headings.title: Classification: Pregestational Versus Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
headings.content: Classification of diabetes in pregnancy is clinically vital because the timing of onset dictates management strategies, baseline risk assessment, and potential fetal complications. Diabetes in pregnancy is broadly classified into two categories: pregestational diabetes mellitus and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Pregestational diabetes encompasses women who had type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus prior to conception. These patients carry a higher risk of first-trimester spontaneous abortions, congenital malformations (due to hyperglycemia during organogenesis), and microvascular complications such as diabetic retinopathy or nephropathy. Conversely, gestational diabetes mellitus is defined as carbohydrate intolerance of variable severity with onset or first recognition during pregnancy, typically manifesting in the second or third trimester when placental hormones peak. GDM is generally associated with macrosomia, birth trauma, and neonatal metabolic disturbances rather than major congenital anomalies, because hyperglycemia develops after organogenesis is complete. Differentiating between these two forms during the initial booking visit is an essential nursing responsibility in Nigerian antenatal clinics, as it guides the urgency of baseline investigations, referral pathways, and individualized care planning for expectant mothers.

headings.title: Maternal and Fetal Risks Associated with Diabetes
headings.content: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus during pregnancy poses severe, multi-systemic risks to both the mother and the developing fetus, necessitating vigilant nursing surveillance. Maternal risks include an increased incidence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy such as pre-eclampsia, spontaneous abortions, urinary tract infections, polyhydramnios due to fetal osmotic diuresis, and an increased likelihood of operative deliveries, including Cesarean sections and instrumental births. Furthermore, obstructed labour can occur secondary to fetal macrosomia, significantly elevating the risk of postpartum hemorrhage and perineal trauma. For the fetus and newborn, the complications are equally profound. Fetal macrosomia (birth weight over 4,000 grams or above the 90th percentile) leads to shoulder dystocia and birth injuries such as Erb's palsy or clavicular fractures. Intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD) can occur late in pregnancy due to placental insufficiency or sudden metabolic imbalances. Neonatally, infants are at high risk for respiratory distress syndrome (because fetal hyperinsulinemia delays surfactant production), transient tachypnea, hypoglycemia immediately after cord clamping, hypocalcemia, and hyperbilirubinemia. Understanding these risks enables nursing students to recognize warning signs early and advocate for timely medical interventions to safeguard maternal-fetal health.

headings.title: Screening, Diagnosis, and Antenatal Assessment
headings.content: Early and accurate screening, diagnosis, and ongoing antenatal assessment are the cornerstones of mitigating diabetic complications in pregnancy. Screening protocols generally begin at the first antenatal booking visit. For women with risk factors (such as a previous history of GDM, family history of diabetes, advanced maternal age, obesity, or history of macrosomia), fasting blood glucose or random blood glucose tests are performed to identify pregestational diabetes. Universal or selective screening for gestational diabetes typically occurs between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation using an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT), such as the 75-gram, 2-hour OGTT. Antenatal assessment involves regular monitoring of maternal blood pressure, urinalysis for protein and glucose, and serial weight checks. Fetal surveillance is equally critical; it includes regular abdominal palpation for fundal height measurement, ultrasound scans for dating, anomaly scanning at 18-20 weeks, and growth scans in the third trimester. Doppler velocimetry and cardiotocography (CTG) or biophysical profiles (BPP) are employed to assess fetal well-being in the presence of poorly controlled diabetes or vascular complications, ensuring timely delivery planning.

headings.title: Glycemic Control and Medical Management
headings.content: Achieving optimal glycemic control is the primary therapeutic goal in managing diabetes during pregnancy to prevent adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. Medical management begins with medical nutrition therapy (MNT) and structured physical exercise, which are prescribed to all clients. Registered dieticians or trained nurses counsel mothers on balanced diets with controlled carbohydrate intake, frequent small meals, and adequate caloric distribution to prevent ketosis and postprandial hyperglycemia. If lifestyle modifications fail to maintain target blood glucose levels (typically fasting blood glucose below 5.3 mmol/L and 1-hour postprandial below 7.8 mmol/L), pharmacological therapy is initiated. Insulin therapy remains the gold standard and safest pharmacological agent in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta in clinically significant amounts. Regimens often combine intermediate-acting and rapid-acting insulins administered via multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion. Oral hypoglycemic agents, specifically metformin and glyburide, are increasingly utilized in certain clinical settings after thorough counseling regarding their placental crossing and long-term safety profiles. Nurses play a crucial role in teaching patients self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG), proper insulin injection techniques, and the recognition and treatment of hypoglycemia.

headings.title: Intrapartum Care and Management of Labour
headings.content: Intrapartum care for women with diabetes requires meticulous multidisciplinary planning to ensure maternal safety, prevent birth trauma, and avoid neonatal complications such as birth asphyxia and hypoglycemia. The timing and route of delivery depend on glycemic control, estimated fetal weight, and associated complications like pre-eclampsia. For well-controlled, uncomplicated gestational diabetes, delivery is generally planned around 39 to 40 weeks of gestation. Poorly controlled diabetes, macrosomia, or vascular complications may warrant earlier delivery, sometimes between 37 and 38 weeks, often following assessment of fetal lung maturity if prior to 39 weeks. During labour, tight glycemic control is paramount to prevent neonatal hypoglycemia at birth. Maternal blood glucose levels are monitored hourly via capillary blood glucose testing, and protocols usually involve continuous intravenous infusions of regular insulin alongside dextrose solutions to maintain blood glucose between 4.0 and 7.0 mmol/L. Continuous electronic fetal heart rate monitoring (CTG) is mandatory throughout labour due to the increased risk of intrapartum fetal distress. Nurses must be vigilant for signs of shoulder dystocia during the second stage of labour, ensuring emergency equipment and personnel, including pediatricians and anesthetists, are readily available.

headings.title: Postpartum Care and Neonatal Complications
headings.content: Postpartum care begins immediately following the delivery of the placenta, which marks the sudden withdrawal of placental diabetogenic hormones. Consequently, insulin requirements drop dramatically post-delivery, and women with pregestational diabetes often require significantly lower doses than their pre-pregnancy baseline, while those with GDM usually discontinue antidiabetic medications entirely. Immediate neonatal care focuses on preventing and managing neonatal hypoglycemia. Newborns should be kept warm, initiated on early breastfeeding within the first hour of life, and have their blood glucose levels monitored via heel-prick tests according to hospital protocols. If blood glucose drops below safe thresholds, early supplementation with expressed breast milk or formula may be necessary, and intravenous glucose may be required in severe cases. Furthermore, nurses must educate postpartum mothers about the high risk of recurrent GDM in future pregnancies and the long-term risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus. Therefore, all women with a history of GDM must undergo a follow-up 75-g oral glucose tolerance test at 6 weeks postpartum to reclassify their glucose tolerance status.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Education
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing interventions and patient education are integral to optimizing outcomes for women with diabetes mellitus in pregnancy. Nurses serve as educators, coordinators of care, and emotional supporters for clients navigating a complex medical regimen. Education should cover dietary modifications, emphasizing complex carbohydrates, fiber-rich foods, and portion control tailored to local Nigerian diets and cultural preferences. Nurses must demonstrate and supervise self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) techniques, ensuring clients understand target blood sugar ranges and how to properly document readings in a logbook. Instruction on insulin administration, proper storage, rotation of injection sites, and recognition of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia symptoms is vital. In addition to physical care, psychological support is crucial; dealing with chronic illness during pregnancy can cause anxiety, depression, and stress. Nurses should provide empathetic counseling, encourage family involvement for social support, and connect mothers with community resources. Emphasizing lifestyle changes post-delivery, such as maintaining a healthy weight and engaging in regular exercise, helps reduce the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes for both mother and child.
